Each record is the registry entry and plan row for one unit; the shipping commit registers it in src/data/puzzles.js, writes the plan row to docs/OVERNIGHT-PLAN.md, bumps livePuzzles, and removes the record. units.oneLiner: Store a height in every node, allow the two children of any node to differ in height by at most one, and repair a broken node on the way back up with a single or double rotation at the lowest place it breaks: the height stays under 1.44 log2 n for any arrival order, an insertion needs at most one rotation, and the sorted input that turns a plain tree into a list builds the perfectly balanced floor instead.
units.description: The AVL tree with height-balance rotations on 20,000 keys against a Python set referee (in-order walk, every lookup, heights and balance factors audited at every node): height 17 under random arrival against the bound 20.3 and the floor 15, 4,732 single and 4,708 double rotations with never more than one per insertion, height 15 under sorted arrival at one rotation per insertion, 0.369 rotations per deletion; lookups at 14.11 node visits against 14.29 for a left-leaning red-black tree (height 21), 17.79 for a treap (height 33), and 18.03 for the plain tree (height 38); and the plain tree on sorted keys at height 4,000 and 2,053 visits per lookup as the negative example.
units.time: O(log n) worst case per operation
units.plan_row: AVL tree × Height-balance rotations. Puzzle 165, data-structures (problemSlug ordered-dictionary, the atlas problem page carrying "Strictly balanced dictionary"). The bench swap: Quicksort × Random pivot was queued at F158 but overlaps two live lessons (quicksort-median-of-three and quickselect-random-pivot, which already builds McIlroy's adversary and the random pivot), so the queue moved to algorithms with no live unit yet. Solution avl_tree_height_balance_rotations.py (1.8s, prints OK): the AVL tree with per-call rebalancing counts and a full audit (search order, stored heights, balance factors), a plain BST, a treap, and Sedgewick's left-leaning red-black tree with its own rule audit, one workload (20,000 inserts, 2,000 lookups half absent inside the key range, 6,666 deletes, 6,666 reinserts) shadowed by a Python set at every checkpoint. ORACLES: (1) the set referee on every structure; (2) the height theorem at five sizes: height 17 at n = 20,000 under the bound 1.4405 log2(n + 2) - 0.328 = 20.3 and at or above the floor 15; sorted arrival builds height 15; (3) at most one rebalancing on each of 20,000 insertions (4,732 single, 4,708 double); deletions 0.369 rotations each, at most 3 rebalancings on one; (4) the race: lookup visits AVL 14.11 / LLRB 14.29 / treap 17.79 / plain 18.03, heights 17 / 21 / 33 / 38, rotations per insert 0.707 / 1.198 / 1.980 / 0, per delete 0.379 / 15.307 / 0.968 / 0; sorted arrival AVL 13.88 visits, LLRB 13.88, treap 19.66; (5) the plain tree on sorted keys: height 4,000 at n = 4,000, 2,053 visits per lookup. Honest: the plain tree is only 30% worse on random lookups (the rule buys the worst case); the LLRB delete cost is the variant's, and the card states the classic three-rotation bound; author correction recorded (single and double rotations nearly equal on random input, not rare). Cards: self, Red-black tree, Treap (live lesson badge), Splay tree (all algoName). neverUse: a plain BST on keys arriving in order. Figure: the double rotation before and after, beside bars of measured heights against the bound and the floor; cite Adelson-Velsky and Landis 1962, Knuth TAOCP 3 6.2.3, Guibas and Sedgewick FOCS 1978 DOI 10.1109/SFCS.1978.3. Viz AvlTreeViz: the same keys (14 shuffled, 18 ascending) into an AVL tree and a plain tree side by side, one per tick, the rotated node ringed red, heights against the bound and the floor; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles x 32 ticks, 0 invariant breaks; stepMs 650, holdTicks rests. Preserved narration: Aoede + Algieba.

units.oneLiner: Walk the whole game tree in self-play, and at every information set add, for each action, the gain it would have had over the strategy played, weighted by how likely the opponent and chance were to bring the game there; next iteration play each action in proportion to its positive regret: the average of everything played converges to a Nash equilibrium at the rate of one over the square root of the iterations, with no learning rate and no linear program.
units.description: Counterfactual regret minimization with regret matching on Kuhn poker (12 information sets, exact value -1/18): after 10,000 iterations the average strategy has value -0.0555 and exploitability 0.0015 by an exact best-response referee, inside the measured regret bound 0.0059, and sits on Kuhn's closed-form family (a jack bet 0.216, a king bet 0.668 against 3 alpha = 0.648, a queen call 0.337 against 1/3); exploitability 0.0911, 0.0233, 0.0065, 0.0015 at 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000 iterations; rock-paper-scissors and biased pennies within 0.01 of their textbook answers; CFR+ 0.0049 and fictitious play 0.0068 at 1,000 iterations, outcome-sampling MCCFR 0.0450 at an equal budget of 58,000 nodes; determinized minimax exploitable for 0.167 a hand as the negative example.
units.time: one full tree walk per iteration; error falls as 1/sqrt(T)
units.space: two numbers per action per information set

units.plan_row: Counterfactual regret minimization × Regret-matching updates. Puzzle 166, search-constraints-games (problemSlug extensive-form-solving, the atlas problem page carrying "Imperfect-information equilibria"). Solution counterfactual_regret_minimization_regret_matching_updates.py (1.2s, prints OK): a generic extensive-form engine (Kuhn poker and a matrix-game class), vanilla CFR with three reach probabilities, CFR+ (floored regrets, alternating updates, linear averaging), outcome-sampling MCCFR with epsilon exploration, full-width fictitious play with realization-weighted mixing, determinized minimax (PIMC), an exact best-response traversal (decisions made once per information set over all member histories), and exploitability as the mean of the two best-response values. ORACLES: (1) Kuhn's closed form: value -0.0555 against -1/18 after 10,000 iterations (580,000 nodes), alpha = P(bet | J) 0.216 in [0, 1/3], P(bet | K) 0.668 against 3 alpha 0.648, P(call | Q facing bet) 0.337 against 1/3, P(bet | J after check) 0.336 against 1/3, P(call | Q after check-bet) 0.554 against alpha + 1/3 = 0.549; (2) exploitability 0.0015 under the measured regret bound (R0 + R1) / T = 0.0059 and under the Zinkevich theorem bound 0.339; falling 0.0911 / 0.0233 / 0.0065 / 0.0015 at 10 / 100 / 1,000 / 10,000; (3) rock-paper-scissors (0.333, 0.329, 0.338) exploitability 0.0058 and biased pennies P(heads) 0.405 against 2/5, value 0.200 against 1/5, both at 20,000 iterations; (4) the race at 1,000 iterations: CFR 0.0065 (58,000 nodes), CFR+ 0.0049 (116,000), fictitious play 0.0068 (116,000), MCCFR 0.0450 at the same 58,000 nodes (5,368 sampled iterations; 0.1058 at 1,000); (5) determinized minimax exploitable for 0.1667, both players losing 0.167 a hand to a best response. Honest: on Kuhn the CFR+ gain is modest and the page says the speedups are a large-game story; author correction recorded (MCCFR expected to win at equal node budget, measured worse). Cards: self, CFR+, Monte Carlo CFR, Fictitious play (all algoName). neverUse: determinized minimax on a bluffing game (strategy fusion). Figure: log-log exploitability curves for four methods with the 1/sqrt(T) slope, beside player one's bet probabilities on the family line 3 alpha; cite Zinkevich et al. NeurIPS 2007, Hart and Mas-Colell Econometrica 2000 DOI 10.1111/1468-0262.00153, Kuhn 1950. Viz CfrViz: live CFR on Kuhn poker, 25 iterations per tick for 80 ticks from a seeded random start, bars of the current and average strategies against the family targets, and the exploitability curve on a log scale with the 1/sqrt(T) slope, computed each tick by the exact best response; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles x 80 ticks; stepMs 180, holdTicks rests. Preserved narration: Aoede + Algieba.

units.oneLiner: Keep a bracket that provably holds the root, propose the next point from the sideways parabola through the last three (the secant when two coincide), and take it only if it stays inside the bracket and is less than half the step before last, falling back to the midpoint otherwise: superlinear on smooth functions, never worse than about the square of bisection's count on any continuous one.
units.description: Brent's method with inverse quadratic interpolation on nine bracketed problems at tolerance 1e-12, every answer checked against a bisection run to the last bit and the published digits: 7 to 9 evaluations on each of six smooth roots (49 in total against 253 for bisection, 62 for Illinois, 54 for Dekker, 144 for Ridders), measured interpolation order 1.88 and 2.08, 33 on the signed cube root that breaks Newton (doubling its error each step) and the secant, 18 on e^x - 1 over [-40, 60] against 109 for Illinois and a false convergence for the secant at x = 60, and an honest loss on the triple root (102 against 42 for bisection), all inside the guarantee of 1,670 to 2,257.
units.time: one evaluation per step; order about 1.84 on smooth f
units.space: three points and two step sizes

units.plan_row: Brent's method × Inverse quadratic interpolation. Puzzle 167, numerical (problemSlug root-finding, the atlas problem page carrying "Robust root finding"). Solution brents_method_inverse_quadratic_interpolation.py (0.1s, prints OK): the classic zeroin with a step-kind trace, bisection, Illinois regula falsi, the plain secant, Newton from the midpoint, Ridders, and Dekker (each with its canonical stop, plus an unsafe step-size stop measured on purpose), a counting wrapper (a derivative counts as one evaluation), nine problems (cos x = x, Wallis's cubic, sqrt 2, e, the omega constant, sin x = x/2, a signed cube root, e^x - 1 on [-40, 60], the triple root (x - 0.3)^3) with published roots, and bisection to the last bit as the referee. ORACLES: (1) every bracketing method within 1e-9 of the referee on all nine, Brent within 1e-10; (2) interpolation order on cos x = x: 1.88, 2.08, 1.20; bisection exactly order 1 ratio 1/2; (3) Brent under (log2((b - a)/tol) + 1)^2 = 1,670 to 2,257 on every function and under 3x bisection on the hard three, under a third of bisection on each smooth one; (4) the race, evaluations: smooth six totals Brent 49 / bisection 253 / Illinois 62 / Dekker 54 / Ridders 144 (82 on Wallis under the bracket criterion), secant 48 and Newton 64 where they converge; cube root Brent 33 (0 iqi, 31 secant, bisection fallbacks) / bisection 43 / Illinois 34 / Dekker 34 / Ridders 40 / secant and Newton fail; e^x - 1 wide: Brent 18 (2 iqi, 8 secant, 6 bisection) / bisection 49 / Illinois 109 / Dekker 16 / Ridders 20 / Newton 32 / secant stops at x = 60 after 3 evaluations with error 40; triple root: Brent 102 (43 iqi, 29 secant, 28 bisection) / bisection 42 / Illinois 111 / Dekker 168 / Ridders 68 / secant 92 / Newton 126; (5) Newton on the cube root from 0.4: 0.1, 0.7, -0.5, 1.9, exactly doubling; the step criterion on the wide bracket: Illinois 4 evaluations error 40, Dekker 3 evaluations error 40, Ridders fine. Honest: Brent loses the triple root to bisection and Ridders, and Dekker is nearly as fast on smooth functions; author correction recorded (Dekker expected to crawl on the wide bracket, measured fast). Cards: self, Bisection method, Ridders' method, Newton's method (live lesson badge) (all algoName). neverUse: an unbracketed method stopped by the size of its step. Figure: rows of step-kind squares for three functions beside bars of smooth-six totals; cite Brent 1973 ch. 4, Dekker 1969, Forsythe-Malcolm-Moler 1977, Alefeld-Potra-Shi TOMS 1995 DOI 10.1145/210089.210111. Viz BrentViz: zeroin one evaluation per tick on cos x - x, the signed cube root, or the wide e^x - 1 (cycling), the bracket shaded, a, b, c marked, the step kind colored, bracket width on a log scale; NODE-VERIFIED 21 cycles, bracket held the root on every tick; stepMs 700, holdTicks rests. Preserved narration: Aoede + Algieba.

units.oneLiner: Give each vertex the smallest color its colored neighbors have not used, taking the vertices in the order that is hardest to fool: the one whose neighbors already show the most distinct colors goes next, ties broken by the most uncolored neighbors; one pass, at most one more color than the largest degree, and exactly two on any bipartite graph.
units.description: Greedy graph coloring with the DSatur saturation order against an exact branch-and-bound chromatic number on 200 random graphs of 24 vertices: optimal on 129 of 200 (average excess 0.355 colors) against 98 for recursive largest first, 58 for smallest-last, 56 for largest-first, and 18 for a random order; exactly 2 colors on 200 of 200 random bipartite graphs where largest-first needed up to 5; at n = 600, 18 and 75 colors against 20 and 80 for largest-first and 19 and 76 for RLF at a thirteenth to a thirty-sixth of RLF's neighbor scans; and the crown graph K50,50 minus a matching, where largest-first and RLF use 50 colors on a 2-colorable graph and DSatur uses 2.
units.time: O(n^2 + m) with a scan, O((n + m) log n) with a heap

units.plan_row: Greedy graph coloring × DSatur saturation ordering. Puzzle 168, graphs (problemSlug vertex-coloring, the atlas problem page carrying "Vertex coloring"). Solution greedy_graph_coloring_dsatur_saturation_ordering.py (0.7s, prints OK): the greedy pass with a scan counter, largest-first, smallest-last with degree buckets (reports degeneracy), DSatur, recursive largest first, Brelaz's exact branch and bound, random G(n, p), random connected bipartite graphs, the crown graph, and Mycielski's construction. ORACLES: (1) 200 random graphs n = 24, p in [0.2, 0.6], exact chi (8,207 search nodes total): optimal DSatur 129 / RLF 98 / smallest-last 58 / largest-first 56 / random 18 of 200, average excess 0.355 / 0.545 / 0.845 / 0.825 / 1.430; (2) every coloring proper, every greedy at most Delta + 1, smallest-last at most degeneracy + 1, DSatur exactly 2 on 200 of 200 random bipartite graphs (largest-first up to 5), Mycielski M3 / M4 / M5 chi 3 / 4 / 5 recovered by the exact solver and hit by every method; (3) G(600, 0.1): clique bound 4, Delta + 1 = 89, DSatur 18 colors (216,282 scans), RLF 19 (2,601,807), largest-first 20 (35,982), smallest-last 21 (71,964), random 22; G(600, 0.5): clique 10, Delta + 1 = 335, DSatur 75 (359,644), RLF 76 (12,832,354), largest-first 80 (179,344), smallest-last 81 (358,688), random 85; (4) crown graph K50,50 minus a matching: largest-first 50, RLF 50, smallest-last 2, DSatur 2. Honest: DSatur is wrong by a color on 71 of 200 small graphs, and the viz's random cycles include ties with largest-first (seed 20261014 opens with 4 against 5 at chi 4; seed 20261010 would have opened with a one-color loss, so the seed was chosen by a scan and the page says the order is not always better); author correction recorded (the draft hedged that RLF would use the fewest colors on dense graphs; measured one behind DSatur on both instances, not generalized). Cards: self, Recursive largest first, Backtracking coloring, Smallest-last ordering (greedy, algoName Greedy graph coloring). neverUse: a static order on the crown graph. Figure: the six-plus-six crown graph colored by largest-first (6) and DSatur (2) beside bars of optimal hits of 200; cite Brelaz CACM 1979 DOI 10.1145/359094.359101, Welsh and Powell 1967, Matula and Beck 1983, Johnson 1974. Viz DsaturViz: the same graph colored one vertex per tick by DSatur (left) and largest-first (right), random 20-vertex graphs with the exact chi computed at scene start on even cycles and the 8+8 crown graph on odd cycles; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles, every coloring proper on every tick; stepMs 600, holdTicks rests. Preserved narration: Aoede + Algieba.
